detailed_rationale:
Supreme Petrochem is a polystyrene, expandable-polystyrene (EPS) and styrenics compounds manufacturer, a joint venture between The Supreme Industries and the Rajan Raheja Group, with styrene monomer as its key input. This is a genuinely cyclical, spread-driven petrochemical business (matching our Cyclical tag): operating margin swung from 6% (Dec-2025) to 19% (Jun-2026) in consecutive quarters, and net profit followed suit - Rs.31 Cr (Dec-2025) to Rs.169 Cr (Mar-2026) to Rs.238 Cr (Jun-2026), the strongest quarter shown. That is a genuine styrene-to-polystyrene spread recovery (input-output margin cycle), not an acquisition or consolidation artifact, but it is exactly the kind of number that should not be naively annualized - petrochemical spreads are volatile and historically mean-revert once new capacity or feedstock costs shift the cycle.

The balance sheet is a clear strength: essentially debt-free (Rs.133 Cr borrowings against Rs.2,339 Cr reserves), promoter holding has risen steadily for almost a decade (60.84% in Mar-2017 to 64.24% now, no pledge disclosed), and dividend payout has been maintained at a generous 60%. ROE of ~13.7% is respectable but was earned across a period that included the weak Dec-2025 quarter, so the current run-rate ROE (annualizing the strong Jun-2026 quarter) would look considerably higher - another reason not to take the trailing multiple at face value without adjusting for where in the cycle the company currently sits.

Reverse-DCF: at ~27x trailing earnings, the multiple looks reasonable if you use blended full-cycle earnings, but would look considerably richer if the market is extrapolating the exceptionally strong Jun-2026 quarter as the new normal - the appropriate discipline here is to price the business on a normalized, cycle-adjusted earnings power rather than the most recent spread-driven print.
recommendation_rationale: Quant reads Hold on both lenses. My own work agrees: the balance sheet is debt-free, promoter conviction is high and rising, and the recent margin recovery is a genuine (if cyclical) business improvement rather than a data artifact - there's no basis for a Sell, and no methodology gap or coin-flip tension warranting escalation, just an ordinary cyclical business that should be valued on normalized earnings.
summary: Supreme Petrochem manufactures polystyrene and EPS plastics used in packaging, insulation and appliances, with a debt-free balance sheet and rising promoter ownership. Profitability swings significantly with input-output price spreads - margins nearly tripled over the last two quarters - so recent strong results should be read as a cyclical recovery rather than a new permanent run-rate. We rate it a Hold.
positive_para: The balance sheet is debt-free, promoter holding has risen steadily for almost a decade (a strong conviction signal from a well-regarded industrial JV), and the company has just delivered a sharp margin recovery (6% to 19% operating margin in two quarters) that shows real operating leverage when the spread environment is favorable. A 60% dividend payout also rewards shareholders directly rather than requiring the cycle to turn favorably for returns to show up.
negative_para: This is a genuinely cyclical, spread-driven commodity plastics business - the swing from a Rs.31 Cr to a Rs.238 Cr quarterly profit in two quarters shows how much of the current earnings power depends on where styrene-to-polystyrene spreads happen to sit today, and that can reverse just as quickly if feedstock costs rise or new capacity (domestic or Asian) compresses margins again. Valuing the stock off the most recent, unusually strong quarter risks overpaying for what may prove to be a cyclical peak rather than a sustainable new level of profitability.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~27x trailing earnings, the multiple is reasonable on a full-cycle, blended-earnings basis for a debt-free petrochemical franchise, but would look considerably richer if the market is extrapolating the exceptionally strong Jun-2026 quarter (19% operating margin) as sustainable - fair to somewhat rich depending on where the spread cycle goes from here, not clearly cheap. Growth is well below the 25% hypergrowth threshold, so no dilution/ROE-tier note applies.
